{{Short description|Geometric minimal hypersurface}}
In [[geometry]] and [[geometric measure theory]], the '''Simons cone''' refers to a specific [[Minimal surface|minimal]] [[hypersurface]] in <math>\mathbb R^8</math> that plays a crucial role in resolving [[Bernstein's problem]] in higher dimensions. It is named after American mathematician [[Jim Simons]].

==Definition==
The Simons cone is defined as the [[hypersurface]] given by the equation
:<math>S = \{x \in \mathbb R^8 | x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 + x_4^2 = x_5^2 + x_6^2 + x_7^2 + x_8^2 \} \subset \mathbb R^8</math>.
This 7-dimensional [[cone (mathematics)|cone]] has the distinctive property that its [[mean curvature]] vanishes at every point except at the origin, where the cone has a [[singularity (mathematics)|singularity]].<ref name="BDG">Bombieri, E., De Giorgi, E., and Giusti, E. (1969). "Minimal cones and the Bernstein problem". ''[[Inventiones Mathematicae]]'', 7: 243-268.</ref><ref name="Philippis-2009">G. De Philippis, E. Paolini (2009). [https://www.numdam.org/item/RSMUP_2009__121__233_0.pdf "A short proof of the minimality of Simons cone"]. ''Rendiconti del Seminario Matematico della Università di Padova'', 121. pp. 233-241</ref>

== Applications ==
{{See also|Bernstein's problem}}
The classical Bernstein theorem states that any minimal graph in <math>\mathbb R^3</math> must be a plane. This was extended to <math>\mathbb R^4</math> by [[Wendell Fleming]] in 1962 and [[Ennio De Giorgi]] in 1965, and to dimensions up to <math>\mathbb R^5</math> by [[Frederick J. Almgren Jr.]] in 1966 and to <math>\mathbb R^8</math> by [[Jim Simons]] in 1968. The existence of the Simons cone as a minimizing cone in <math>\mathbb R^8</math> demonstrated that the Bernstein theorem could not be extended to <math>\mathbb R^9</math> and higher dimensions. Bombieri, De Giorgi, and [[Enrico Giusti]] proved in 1969 that the Simons cone is indeed area-minimizing, thus providing a negative answer to the Bernstein problem in higher dimensions.<ref name="BDG"/><ref name="Philippis-2009"/>
